overview:
In Jain philosophical literature, the phrase “infinite energy” does not refer to a physical or technological concept such as perpetual motion or limitless fuel. Instead, it is a metaphysical category describing the inherent, boundless capacities of the *jīva* (sentient soul) when fully unobstructed by karma. Jainism holds that every soul possesses *ananta-śakti*—infinite power—alongside other infinitudes such as infinite perception (*ananta-darśana*), infinite knowledge (*ananta-jñāna*), and infinite bliss (*ananta-sukha*). These qualities are eternally present but obscured by karmic bondage. When karmic veils are removed at the highest spiritual stage (*kevala-jñāna*), the soul’s infinite energies manifest completely.

In cosmological contexts, Jain texts also describe the universe as beginningless and endless, governed by eternal substances (*dravya*) and their modes (*paryāya*). Energy, in the modern scientific sense, is not a separate substance in Jain ontology. Instead, activity, motion, and transformation arise from the interaction of *jīva*, *pudgala* (matter), *dharma-dravya* (principle of motion), *adharma-dravya* (principle of rest), *ākāśa* (space), and *kāla* (time). Matter (*pudgala*) is capable of infinite combinations and transformations, but not infinite creation ex nihilo. Thus, Jainism does not endorse the idea of physically infinite energy production; rather, it affirms the soul’s infinite spiritual potency.

Across Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, the concept of infinite energy is consistently tied to liberation (*mokṣa*) and the soul’s natural attributes. Commentaries emphasize that these infinitudes are not metaphorical but ontological: they describe the soul’s real, eternal capacities once karmic obscurations are removed. Modern Jain scholars often compare this to the idea of an unbounded consciousness rather than a physical energy source. The term therefore serves as a bridge between metaphysics, ethics, and soteriology, illustrating the ultimate goal of Jain practice: the full manifestation of the soul’s infinite qualities.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Liberation is the state of infinite knowledge, infinite perception, infinite conduct, and infinite bliss.
primary_sources.notes: TS 10.1 (Tier A). This sutra establishes the four infinitudes of the liberated soul. While it does not explicitly use the phrase 'infinite energy,' the tradition interprets these infinitudes as the soul’s unobstructed powers.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra Jīva-kāṇḍa
primary_sources.author: Nemichandra Siddhānta Chakravartin
primary_sources.translation: The powers of the soul are infinite.
primary_sources.notes: Digambara text (Tier A/B). This passage describes the soul’s inherent infinite capacities, often cited in discussions of ananta-śakti.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples
primary_sources.notes: Śvetāmbara canon (Tier A). Here *vīrya* refers to spiritual vigor or potency, not physical energy. Commentaries expand this into the doctrine of infinite spiritual power in the liberated state.

misconceptions.myth: Jainism teaches that the physical universe contains infinite usable energy.
misconceptions.reality: Jain ontology does not treat energy as a separate substance and does not claim that matter can produce infinite physical energy. The infinitude applies to the soul’s spiritual capacities, not to material processes.

misconceptions.myth: Infinite energy in Jainism means humans can attain supernatural physical powers.
misconceptions.reality: The doctrine refers to the liberated soul’s infinite spiritual qualities. It does not imply that embodied beings can access limitless physical strength or violate natural laws.

misconceptions.myth: Infinite energy is a metaphor for enthusiasm or moral effort.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain metaphysics, the soul’s infinitudes are literal ontological attributes revealed upon liberation, not symbolic expressions of human motivation.
